# How to Edit a Photo with Aperture | Media Manipulator Tutorial

- Route: `/tutorials/aperture`

## Summary

Step-by-step Aperture tutorial: open a photo, fix light and color, make one color pop, edit with masks, heal blemishes, export at full resolution, reuse looks and batch-apply.

## Details

How to edit a photo with Aperture
Aperture is Media Manipulator's non-destructive photo editor. Every change you make is an adjustment layer stacked over the untouched original, so you can reorder, mask, fade or delete any step later, and the file you opened is never altered. The preview is drawn on your graphics card from a 1920 px copy; the export is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas. This guide walks through one edit from opening a photo to applying the finished look to a whole set, using the panel and slider names you will see in the editor.
1. Open a photo
Open Aperture from its tool page or from any photo tool page on Media Manipulator. The editor takes over the whole screen with no ads. Drop a photo onto the open screen or press Choose a photo. Once it is decoded you get the preview in the middle, the Panels and Layers tabs on one side, and a live histogram showing red, green, blue and luminance. Hold the backslash key at any time to see the original, or turn on Split view to compare halves.
You can open JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF and BMP files. Your browser decodes the common web formats on its own. HEIC, HEIF, TIFF and BMP need an account, because the server makes a preview copy before the editor can show them.
Without an account, the photo and your edits stay in this browser's storage and nothing is uploaded until you export, select a subject or heal. Guests keep one photo at a time; opening a second one replaces the saved project, and the editor asks before it does so.
Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block. The project opens on any device and autosaves as you work, with the saved state shown in the top bar.
The original file is never changed. Every adjustment is a layer over it, with its own opacity from 0 to 100 percent, a blend mode of normal, luminosity or color, and an optional mask. You can stack up to 64 layers, and the History panel lists every step.
2. Fix light and color with Basic
Most photos need the Basic panel first. It groups the global sliders into Exposure, Light, Tone, White balance and Color sections, each of which becomes its own adjustment layer the moment you move a slider. Work from the top down: get overall brightness right, then recover highlights and shadows, then correct the color cast, then decide how much color you want. Watch the histogram while you drag; clipping shows up as a pile-up at either end.
Exposure (EV) runs from -5 to +5 stops and multiplies every pixel by two to the power of the value, so +1 doubles the light. Offset adds or subtracts a flat amount from -0.5 to 0.5, and Gamma from 0.1 to 10 bends the midtones. Light holds Brightness and Contrast from -100 to 100.
Tone has Highlights, Shadows, Whites and Blacks. Pull Highlights down to bring back a bright sky, raise Shadows to open a dark face, and use Whites and Blacks to set where the brightest and darkest points land. Each slider targets its own part of the luminance range instead of moving everything.
White balance has Temperature and Tint. Temperature shifts the photo toward blue or amber; Tint shifts it toward green or magenta. Indoor shots under warm bulbs usually need Temperature pulled toward blue, and fluorescent light often needs a little magenta Tint. Judge the result on something that should be neutral gray or white.
Nothing here is permanent. Undo and redo are on the top bar and the keyboard, the History panel jumps back to any earlier state, and you can save a named snapshot of a version you like for the rest of the session. Lower a layer's opacity to apply half of an adjustment instead of redoing it.
3. Make one color pop
The selective color effect, where one color stays and everything else turns gray, lives in the Color (HSL) panel. You can get there in one step with a built-in look or build it by hand. The hand-built route gives you control over exactly which hues survive and how soft the edge between color and gray is, which matters for things like skin that sits between reds and yellows.
In the Looks panel, choose Color pop: red, yellow, green, cyan, blue or magenta. The look adds a Color (HSL) layer on top of your edits that desaturates every range except the one you picked. If it is not what you wanted, a single Undo removes the whole look.
To build it yourself, open Color (HSL). Each of the six ranges, Reds, Yellows, Greens, Cyans, Blues and Magentas, has a Gray except this chip. Press the chip on the color you want to keep and the other five ranges drop to minus 100 saturation in one move.
If the color you want to keep is not one of the six, use Pick a color from the photo to add a custom range with the eyedropper. Each range has Width and Feather controls, so you can widen it to include neighboring hues or soften the border so the transition does not look cut out.
Then fine-tune the surviving color with its own Hue, Saturation and Lightness sliders. A little extra Saturation and a touch less Lightness usually makes the kept color read stronger against gray. If the look is too strong overall, lower the layer's opacity in the Layers tab rather than redoing it.
4. Edit only part of the photo with masks
Any adjustment layer can carry a mask, which limits where it applies. Select the layer in the Layers tab, open Masks and add a component. White areas of the mask get the full adjustment, black areas get none, and gray areas get a proportion. Mask view switches between off, a colored overlay on the photo and the mask alone, so you can see exactly what you are affecting before you start moving sliders.
There are six mask kinds: Linear gradient for a sky or a floor, Radial for a spotlight around a point, Brush for painting by hand with adjustable size and an erase toggle, Luminosity range for the bright or dark parts only, Color range for pixels of a chosen color, and Select subject.
A mask can hold several components, and each one is set to Add, Subtract or Intersect. A common recipe is a Linear gradient over the sky with a Subtract Brush that protects a building that pokes into it. Mask feather softens the edge, Mask strength scales the whole thing, and Invert flips it.
Color range uses the same eyedropper idea as the HSL panel: pick a color, shift-click to add up to eight more, and raise Fuzziness to include nearby shades. It is a quick way to darken only a blue sky or warm only the skin tones without painting anything.
Select subject asks our GPU to find the main person or object and returns a soft-edged mask in a few seconds. It is the one mask kind that uploads the photo and counts as an everyday operation on your plan; an identical repeat is a free cache hit. Every other mask kind is computed in your browser and costs nothing.
5. Heal spots and blemishes
Dust on a sensor, a pimple, a stray wire or a bit of litter can all go through the Heal panel. Unlike the sliders, healing is a generative step: our server fills the painted area with new pixels that match the surroundings. It still lands in your layer stack and your history, so you can undo it or hold backslash to compare with the original, but it is the one tool in this guide that costs an AI operation.
Pick the Spot brush and paint over each mark you want gone. Make the dab a little larger than the spot itself so the fill has clean texture to blend into. The panel counts the spots you have marked, and Clear spots starts over if you change your mind before pressing Heal.
Press Heal when the spots are marked. The photo and the painted area go to our GPU, where the LaMa inpainting model fills the marked areas; this can take up to a minute on a large file. When it comes back, the result is applied as a step in your history with an Undo available.
Each press of Heal is one AI operation on your plan, no matter how many spots you painted, so mark everything first and press once. The daily allowance per plan is listed on the pricing page. Painting spots, clearing them and undoing a heal cost nothing.
Healing sits in your layer stack like everything else, so the color and tone layers you add afterward apply to the healed result, and Undo or the History panel takes it back out. For red eyes in flash portraits there is a separate Red-eye panel that needs no AI at all.
6. Export at full resolution
Press Export on the top bar when the edit is finished. The preview you have been working on is a 1920 px copy drawn on your graphics card; the export is a server job that renders the original at its full size with the same formulas, so the two agree to within a few 8-bit levels at most. The result is downloaded as a new file named after the original with (retouched) added, and the original file is untouched.
Choose JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF, set Quality from 1 to 100 where it applies, and choose whether to Keep or Strip the metadata. Stripping removes the EXIF block, including camera settings and any GPS location, which is usually what you want before posting a photo publicly.
Max size offers Original, 12, 24, 64 and 120 megapixels. The dialog estimates the file size for your choice: a JPG at quality 92 is about 0.45 MB per megapixel, so a 6000 x 4000 photo at 24 MP comes out near 10.8 MB, while WebP is around 0.3 MB and AVIF around 0.2 MB per megapixel.
Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block. The job runs on our server, which renders with NumPy and OpenCV, encodes with ImageMagick and offers the file for download when it is done.
One export is one everyday operation on your plan, and you can run Export again with different settings afterward, for example a full-size TIFF for printing and a 12 MP WebP for the web. Previewing, every slider, every non-AI mask, looks and undo are free and unlimited.
7. Save and reuse looks
A look in Aperture is a saved group of adjustment layers. The Looks panel ships with 18 built-in looks plus Auto, and it is also where your own presets live. Saving a preset captures the layers you choose with their current values, so the warm, slightly faded treatment you dialed in for one photo can be dropped onto the next one in a single click, and still comes in as editable layers rather than a baked-in filter.
The built-in looks are grouped as Color, Black & white, Film and Fix, and include the six Color pop looks, Black & white film, High-contrast black & white, Warm, Cool, Matte, Fade, Vivid, Punch, Cross-process, Vintage, Portrait soften, Landscape and Auto. Use the filter box to find one by name.
Applying a look adds its adjustments as a named group on top of what you already have instead of replacing your work. That means you can stack Warm over your own Basic corrections, open the group in the Layers tab to tweak individual sliders, and remove the whole look with one Undo.
Choose Save current edits as a preset, give it a name and tick the adjustments to include. It appears under My presets. When you are signed in your presets are stored on your account and follow you to your other devices; without an account they are stored in this browser. You can rename or delete them from the same panel.
Export presets writes your saved presets to a JSON file; Import presets reads one back in. Use this to move presets to another browser or computer, to keep a backup, or to share a look with someone else who uses Aperture on Media Manipulator.
8. Apply the same edits to more photos
When several photos from the same shoot need the same treatment, you do not have to repeat the edit. Finish one photo, open the Export dialog and choose Apply to more photos. It takes the entire layer stack of the current project, including masks and healing you have already done on this photo, and renders it onto the other files you pick with the export settings you chose, then hands you everything as one download.
Apply to more photos is available only when you are signed in; the dialog asks guests to sign in. Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block. Pick more than your plan allows and the extra files are left out, and the dialog says how many.
Each chosen photo is first created as its own project in your account, one after another, so the originals and their edits are kept like any other project. Then a single batch job renders them all on the server, and the dialog shows each photo move from Preparing to Rendering with a percentage to Done.
When the renders finish, press Download as ZIP. The archive is built in your browser from the finished files, so nothing extra is uploaded and you get one file to save instead of a dozen separate downloads. If a file could not be added, the dialog tells you how many are missing.
If a photo fails, the others are not held up. The dialog shows how many failed and offers a Retry button for just those files, and the ZIP can be built again once they finish. Exports count as everyday operations on your plan, so check the pricing page before running a large batch.
